title: Starting a union: seven members and a purpose
author: Editorial Desk
summary: How workers can register a trade union: Article 19, the seven-member rule, the ten per cent or 100 workers test, steps, recognition and affiliation.
body:
Every union begins in the same way: a handful of workers who are tired of facing a problem alone. Under the Constitution, they are free to join together. Article 19(1)(c) guarantees citizens the right to form associations or unions or co-operative societies, and Article 19(4) allows the State to impose only reasonable restrictions on that right in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, public order or morality ([Constitution of India, Article 19](https://constitutionofindia.net/articles/article-19-protection-of-certain-rights-regarding-freedom-of-speech-etc/)). Registration is the step that gives the union a legal personality and the ability to act as one. This post explains, in plain terms, how a registered trade union is formed today under the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.

## The legal framework

Trade unions and industrial disputes are subjects on the Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule, which is why both the Centre and the States have a role ([Constitution of India, Concurrent List](https://constitutionofindia.net/schedules/list-iii-concurrent-list/)). The Industrial Relations Code, which came into force with the other three Codes on 21 November 2025, now contains the central law on trade unions, in a chapter on registration, rights and recognition. The Code defines a trade union as a temporary or permanent combination formed mainly to regulate the relations between workers and employers, between workers and workers, or between employers and employers, and it includes a federation of two or more unions.

A union applies for registration to the Registrar of Trade Unions. Which Government's machinery applies depends on the establishment, since each Code speaks of the "appropriate Government": for establishments such as railways, mines and banking it is the Central Government, and for most other employers it is the State Government. If you are unsure, ask your State labour department, since the Central rules apply only where the Centre is the appropriate Government ([Bar & Bench](https://www.barandbench.com/view-point/the-next-phase-of-workforce-compliance-what-the-newly-notified-central-labour-rules-mean-for-employers)).

## The numbers that matter

Section 6 of the Code sets the criteria for registration. In summary:

- **Any seven or more members** of a trade union can apply for registration by signing its rules.
- A union of workers cannot be registered unless, on the date of the application, its members are **at least ten per cent of the workers or one hundred workers, whichever is less**, engaged in the establishment or industry it represents.
- The application does not lapse merely because some applicants drop out, as long as no more than half of the original applicants leave or withdraw in writing.
- A registered union must keep at least the same level of membership throughout, with a minimum of seven members ([Indian Kanoon: Section 6, Industrial Relations Code, 2020](https://future.indiankanoon.org/doc/137035135/)).

Two further points are worth noting. The Registrar may require a change of name if the proposed name is too similar to that of an existing union. And once registered, a union becomes a body corporate under its registered name, with perpetual succession, a common seal and the power to hold property ([Industrial Relations Code summary, Lawrbit](https://www.lawrbit.com/?p=2563)).

Who counts as a "worker" also matters. The Code's definition covers a person doing manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, but excludes people mainly in managerial or administrative roles and supervisors earning above a stated monthly wage, which the text sets at Rs 18,000 or a higher amount notified by the Government. A union of workers should check which of its members fall inside the definition.

## Steps to follow

1. **Meet and agree.** Hold a meeting of interested colleagues and agree on the union's name, its objects (what it exists to do) and its first office-bearers.
2. **Draft the rules.** The rules, or constitution, should cover the name, objects, membership and eligibility, subscription, how officers are elected, the term of office, how meetings are called, how accounts are kept and audited, and how the rules can be amended.
3. **Hold a founding meeting** and record the minutes, with the names and signatures of the members who attend and those who sign the application.
4. **Check the numbers.** Confirm that you meet the seven-member minimum and the ten per cent or one hundred worker rule for your establishment. Keep a list of members with their employee details so that you can show this if asked.
5. **Apply to the Registrar** with the rules, the signed application, the names, addresses and occupations of the officers, and any other documents the rules require. Keep a copy and a dated receipt.
6. **Respond to queries.** The Registrar may ask for corrections or a change of name. Reply in writing and in time.
7. **After registration, run the union properly.** Maintain a membership register, issue receipts for subscriptions, keep accounts, hold the meetings your rules require, and file whatever returns the Registrar requires. Notice boards should carry meeting notices and the audited accounts.

## What registration gives you in practice

Under the Code, a registered union has a route to recognition by the employer for the purpose of negotiation. As summarised by the International Bar Association, if there is only one registered union in an establishment it becomes the negotiating union. If there are several, a union with 51 per cent or more of the workers on the muster roll becomes the sole negotiating union. If none reaches 51 per cent, the employer forms a negotiating council from unions that have at least 20 per cent support ([IBA: India's new Labour Codes, recognition of trade unions](https://www.ibanet.org/India-new-Labour-Codes-recognition-of-trade-unions)). Recognition lasts three years and can be extended to five by mutual agreement.

The Central rules notified in May 2026 add that a registered union with at least 30 per cent membership can be recognised as the negotiating union, subject to verification of membership by secret ballot at the employer's cost, and that establishments with 300 or more workers must provide facilities such as office space to the negotiating union or council ([Mondaq](https://www.mondaq.com/india/employee-rights-labour-relations/1807196/cracking-the-code-ii-the-new-central-labour-rules-at-a-glance)). They also require an employer to inform the secretary of every registered union before a lock-out ([Bar & Bench](https://www.barandbench.com/view-point/the-next-phase-of-workforce-compliance-what-the-newly-notified-central-labour-rules-mean-for-employers)). Different thresholds may apply under State rules, so the safest course is to check your own State's rules.

The right to strike is also tied to the Code. Workers may not strike without giving notice, with summaries describing a 60-day window and a minimum of 14 days from the date of notice ([Lawrbit](https://www.lawrbit.com/?p=2563)). A union should therefore always keep its notices and its authority to call action in order.

## Affiliation

A registered union can choose to affiliate to a federation and a central organisation. BMS describes its own structure as being built from the bottom up: local unions first, then larger unions, State federations and State units, and national industrial federations ([The Onward March of BMS](https://cdn.dbthengadi.in/scan/The_Onward_March_OF_BMS.pdf)). Its pamphlet states that BMS works through 32 All India Industrial Federations and sits on bodies such as the Indian Labour Conference and the Standing Labour Committee ([VVGNLI: BMS at a Glance](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Bharatiya%20Mazdoor%20Sangh%20At%20a%20Glance.pdf)). Affiliation is a decision for the union's own members, taken under its rules and recorded in its minutes. A federation can offer training, legal advice and a place in tripartite forums, which a single small union rarely has.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Registering too early**, before you can show the required share of workers, which risks rejection.
- **Weak rules**, leaving unclear who can be a member or how officers are chosen, and leading to disputes later.
- **No records.** An unrecorded meeting, an unreceipted subscription or an unsigned account is a future dispute.
- **Depending on one person.** A union that relies on a single leader will struggle when he or she retires or is transferred. Spread responsibility across a committee.

## A reminder

A union is a group of people more than a document. Regular meetings, clean accounts and care for every member are what keep it alive. The certificate gives the union a name in law, but the trust of members gives it strength.
